newsitem.title: USA: Jury deadlocked over damages in Food Lion/ABC case.
newsitem.headline: Jury deadlocked over damages in Food Lion/ABC case.

text.p: For the third time in a week, a federal jury said it was deadlocked on whether ABC television unit should pay punitive damages to Food Lion Inc., but a judge ordered the jurors to return to court next week and try again.
"Your Honor, we can't come to an agreement and feel we can go no further," a note signed by all 12 jurors said.

The jury of six men and six women gave the note to U.S. District Judge Carlton Tilley at the end of the panel's fourth consecutive day of deliberations. The jury has spent nearly 23 hours this week weighing evidence in the supermarket chain's fraud lawsuit against ABC.
In 1992, ABC's "PrimeTime Live" broadcast a report that showed pictures of spoiled meat and unsanitary practices at several Food Lion stores.

The Salisbury, N.C.-based company said its sales and stock price plunged after the broadcast, which was based on video obtained by two ABC undercover journalists who wore hidden cameras while briefly working for Food Lion as a deli clerk and meat wrapper.
Food Lion has not challenged the truth of the ABC story, but sued ABC, a unit of Walt Disney Co., and its producers for fraud and trespassing.
The case is being closely watched by major news organizations, which worry that this represents a new way companies have to attack newsgathering, without filing a libel lawsuit.

After reading the note, Tilley informally polled the jury to find out if any believed they might be able to reach a decision after taking a long weekend off. Seven of the jurors raised their hands to indicate "yes" in response to the judge.
He then ordered the panel to return to the courthouse in Greensboro, N.C., on Tuesday, following the federal holiday observing Martin Luther King's birthday on Monday.
"Take the weekend off. Do something that's fun," Tilley told the jurors in an effort to encourage the panel to reach a decision.

On Wednesday, the jury sent two notes to the judge, the second saying the panel was deadlocked 11-to-1 in its deliberations. The note said the jury reached a stalemate because one juror, a woman, was determined not to work with the rest of the panel.
Last month, the jury found ABC liable for fraud and ordered the network to pay actual damages of $1,400.
The panel has had a much more difficult time reaching a unanimous agreement on whether, and how much, ABC and the four producers should be ordered to pay Food Lion in punitive damages.
In a brief discussion with the judge in open court late Friday, the foreman of the panel indicated that deliberations had not gone smoothly.
"There hasn't been a situation where all 12 agree on any aspect of the entire verdict sheet," the unidentified foreman told the judge.
Jurors began deliberations on Tuesday after the judge gave them a 12-page verdict worksheet to fill out in determining if ABC and four of its producers should pay punitive damages.

Earlier in the day, jurors asked to review certain testimony in the trial, including a sworn statement made by ABC attorney Jonathan Barzilay, who approved the network's undercover investigation of Food Lion.

Bill Jeffers, a lawyer for ABC, asked the court out of the jury's presence whether the panel should be forced to reach a consensus, suggesting he was opposed to the measure, but lawyers for Food Lion said they supported the decision, and Tilley declined to change his mind.

Food Lion did not ask for a specific amount in punitive damages, but urged jurors earlier in the trial to set damages high enough to stop news organizations from pursuing future investigative reports that break the law in the process.
Food Lion is a unit of Belgian retailer Ets Delhaize Freres et Cie "LE LION' SA and had 1996 sales of $9 billion.
